newsitem.title: LESOTHO: Army action seen cementing Lesotho's democracy.
newsitem.headline: Army action seen cementing Lesotho's democracy.

text.p: The army's intervention to help the Lesotho government end a police mutiny on Sunday bodes well for the tiny kingdom's struggle to establish a stable democracy, diplomats say.

Over 30 policemen were arrested after the Lesotho Defence Force used heavy gunfire to overpower rebels who had seized the police headquarters in the capital of Maseru. Government reports said there were no casualities.
The government initially told the army to intervene on Thursday, but had to wait until dawn on Sunday for commanders to order troops in.
Western diplomatic sources said the government of Prime Minister Ntsu Mokhehle would now be able to claim a victory in efforts to remain on a democratic path.

"The fact that the military gave its support to the government of the day symbolises a dramatic change in the mindset of the security forces (who now realise) that they cannot do unconstitutional things," one diplomat told Reuters.
"What happened today will change a frame of mind in the army and police who were unsure of their role in this fairly new democracy," he added.
Mokhehle has faced a series of crises since March 1993 when he won the first democratic polls in two decades, with repeated fighting between army factions and police strikes.
Last April he granted amnesty to soldiers who tried to oust his government in 1994 and others who had launched a strike for higher pay.

Eight policemen kicked off the latest threat when they took over the police building in an attempt to resist arrest for the killing of three fellow officers in 1995, demanding they also receive amnesty.
By Sunday, 11 days after the siege began, the mutiny had spread into a strike by Lesotho's 2,000 police officers. It was unclear if they would return to work on Monday.
"The government was limited in actions it could take to enforce the judicial system," another diplomat in Maseru said of the use of the army. "It was right to insist on rule."
However a local chief who visited the shot-up office after the arrests, Khoabane Cheko, told reporters the military action had "disgraced" Lesotho.
"We did not expect this action while there were attempts to negotiate a solution. It shows the government is politically inflexible," said Chief Cheko, who is a senator in Mokhehle's government.
The lawyer representing the eight rebels, Hae Phoofolo, said church groups, non-governmental organisations and politicians has been trying to find a peaceful end to the rebellion.

"I think this whole situation was an over-reaction because there were discussions which would have yielded better fruits," he said at the scene. "It was the wrong thing for the government to use the military to solve problems in this country."

Diplomats said Sunday's use of military force would not affect differences in the ruling Basotho Congress Party, which faces general elections early next year. Political analysts have said the party is split between nationalists and pragmatists who want closer links with South Africa and the region.

The picturesque landlocked mountain kingdom has nearly two million people in an area the size of Belgium. It is heavily dependent on remittances from miners working in South Africa and customs receipts make up about half of government revenue.
